MY Lord Martianus. Morrow. You are sad my Lord. The kings not stirring yet. My beards not so gray as your wits greene. Would you would proue as honest princes as your great graundsire was, or halfe so wise as your elder brother was, theres a Couple of you, Sfoote I am ashamed you should be of the blood royall. You doe not knovv your state, theres Elydure Your elder brother next vnto the King, He plies his booke, vvhen shall you see him trace Lasciuious Archigallo through the streets, And fight with common hacksters hand to hand, To wrest from them their goods and dignityes. Well, well, I haue serued foure kings, And none of all those foure but would haue ventured Their safeties on old Cornwels constancy, But thats all one, now I am cald a dotard, Go to, though now my limbes be starke and stiffe, When Cornwels dead Brittayne I know will want So strong a prop, Alasse I needs must weepe, And shed teares in abundance, when I thinke How Archigallo wrongs his gouernment. Why do you frowne vpon your seruants king, We loue you, and you ought to fauor vs: Will you to Counsel. Heeres petitions, Complaints and controuersies twixt your subiects, Appealing all to you. My Lord, these generall wrongs will draw your highnesse into the common hatred of your subiects. My liedge I know him, he's an honest subiect That hates extortion, vsury, and such sinnes As are too common in this Land of Brittaine. There is a way; but walls haue eares and eyes, Your eare my Lord, and counsell. He must be then deposd. All Cornwells at my becke, Deuonshire our neighbour Is one with vs, you in the North commaund. The oppressed, wrongd, deiected and supprest, Will flocke on all sides to this innovation: The Clergie late despisd, the Nobles scornd, The Commons trode on, and the Law contemnd, Will lend a mutuall and combyned power Vnto this happie change. How, betraide. Ile helpe it all; doe you but sooth me vp, Wele catch them in the trap they lay for vs. Now sir, the king deposd Who shall succeede? Tush, he's too milde to rule. But there are two young princes, hopefull youths And of rare expectation in the Land, Oh would they daigne to beare this weightie charge Betwixt them, and support the regall scepter With ioynt assistance, all our hopes were full. My honord Lord, wele breake it to those princes, Those hopefull youths, at our conuenient leasure. You that our footsteps watcht, Shall in the depth of your owne wiles be catcht. Deposd! did you heare that my Lord. If you refuse it, knowe we are determined To lay it else where. Yonders the King; my soueraigne you haue lost The fall of a braue stagge, he's dead my liedge. VVhat fellowes this? No my liedge not I. Thou art no king of mine, thou art a traytor, Thy life is forfeit by thy stay in Brittaine. VVert thou not banisht? Elidure, If you are wearie of your gouernment, Wele set the Crowne vpon a strangers head Rather then Archigallo. Harke ye Lords, Shall we make him our King we did depose, So might our heads be chopt of, Ile loose mine Ere my poore Country shall endure such wrongs, As that iniurious tyrant plagues her with, VVhat should I say? faith I shall fall a weeping: Therefore speake you. I say that I am sorry he was bad. And now am glad hee's chang'd; his wickednes We punisht, and his goodnes there's great reason Should be rewarded; therefore Lords set on To Yorke then, to his Coronation. Great Queene, Once more the tribute of our bended knees We pay to you, and humbly kisse your hand. Your husband on the suddaine is falne sicke. Looke to the Queene, let vs not loose her to, She breathes, stand of, where be those wemen there, Good Queene that shall be, lends a helping hand, Helpe to vnlace her. He discords taught, that taught thee so to sing. Doe not resigne, good King. Ile keepe still thy Crowne. Tush this for care. Tyrants good subiects kills and traitors spare. Resigne, to whom? Nay make the number euen, And kill me to, for I am pleasd to dye, Rather then this indure. And thats prodigious, I but waite the time To see their sodaine fall that swiftly clime. Shold you set free the Princesse might not she Make vprors in the land, and raise the Commons. In the releasment of the Captiue King. Secure your state by her imprisonment. Or you be scornd by one to you inferior, In generall estimation of the land. By heauen well spyed. That am I. Yet we are enemies, why fight we not With one another, for our generals losse. A third time liue our gratious soueraigne Monarch of England, crowned by these hands. My liege, he tels me heeres a great contention betwixt two noted persons of the Land much spoke of by all states, one some-body Hath brought before your highnes and this presence, An infamous and strange opiniond fellow, Cald No-body, they would intreat your highnes, To heare their matters scand. I but what proofe or lawfull euidence Can you bring forth, that this was done by him. now No-body, vvhat can you say to this. If this be true my liedge, as true it is, Some-body will be found an arrant cheater, Vnlesse he better can acquit himselfe. Here are my liedge bonds forfei • by poore men, Which he releast out of the vsurers hands, And canceld. Leases likewise forfeited, By him repurchast. These peticions, Of many poore men to preferre their sutes. Vnto your highnesse. My liedge you cannot to be seuere in punishing, Those monstrous crimes, the onely staine and blemish To the weale-publike.

I hate all traitors, and had rather die, Then see such wrong done to his soueraignty. Come kill me first. Cornwell and I will beare the selfe same state. My Lord much honor might you win your land To giue release vnto your sister Queene, Being a Lady in the land beloud. Renowne your selfe by being kind to her. Will you be braued by one thats but your equall, Hauing no more then party gouernment. I. Warre is the souldiors haruest it cuts downe. So does Martianus. this way I saw vigenius on the spur. True Brothers in ambition, and in death. To much blood already hath beene spent, Now therefore since the difference in themselues, Is reconsiled in eithers ouerthrow, Let vs be as we were before this Iar, And ioyning hands like honorable frends, Inter their bodyes as becomes their state, And which is rare once more to Elidure, Who now in prison leades a wearied life, With true submission offer Englands Crowne. Of all the charges of tumultuous fate, This is most strange three times to flow in state. Lets heare his accusations, And then how well thou canst aquit thy selfe. Sirha, what can you say to this? Besides strange rumors and false buzzing tales, Of mutinous leesings raisd by No-body.

speeches.Mar,: For the decease of Archigalloes vertues, I vnderstand you Noble minded Cornwell, What generous spirit drawes this Brittish ayre, But droops at Archigalloes gouernement.
And reason Martianus, when the Sunne Struggles to be deliuered from the wombe Of an obscure Eclipse, doth not the earth Mourne to behold his shine envelloped, O Corbonon when I did close thine eyes, I gaue release to Britaines miseries. My lords, and Kings, Tis bootlesse to contend gainst heauen and you, Since without our consent the kings desposd, And we vnable to support his fall, Rather then the whole land should shrinke, You shall haue my assystance in the state. Cornwell hates flattery. I periduras, this way. Then somebodies a knaue. I marrie Nobody what say you to this, See, heere are dangerous Libils gainst the state, And no name to them, therefore nobodies.
The same to you, and you, you are sad my Lordes, your harts I thinke are frosty, for your blood Seemes crvsted in your faces, like the dew In a September morne, how fares the king, Haue you yet bid good morrow to his highnes. My deerest loue, the essence of my soule, And you my honord Lords, the sute you make, Though it be iust for many wrongs imposd, Yet vnto me it seemes an iniurie. VVhat is my greatnes by my brothers fall, But like a starued body nourished With the destruction of the other lymbes. Innumerable are the griefes that waite On horded treasures, then much more on Crownes: The middle path, the golden meane for me, Leaue me obedience, take you Maiestie. I had rather stay his leasure to amend. Carry me to my graue, not to a Throne. Neuer did any lesse desire to raigne Then I, heauen knowes this greatnes is my paine. Tis sweeter to obay. Good brother grieue not, tis against my will, That I am made a King, pray take my place, I had rather be your subiect then your Lord. Leaue that to me? Not from his life I pray. And therein Lords effect my tragedie. Banish him rather, oh sweete spare his life, He is my brother. Oh brother, if you roughly speake, I knowe There is no hope but your sure ouerthrowe, Pray be not angry with me for my loue: To banishment since it must needes be so, His life I giue him whosoere saies no. I hers and all. Alas my brother. Giue them my Crowne, oh giue them all I haue, Thy Throne I reckon but a glorious graue. On to our funerall, tis no matter where, I sinne I knowe in suffering pride so neere. Hearded, goe single him, or couple straight, He will not fall to day, what fellowes this. A banisht man I thinke, My brother Archigallo, ist not so. Tis Archigallo man. Yet looke vpon his misery, his teares Argue repentance; thinke not honourd Lords The feare of dangers waiting on my Crowne Makes me so willing to resigne the same, For I am lou'd I know, but iustice bids I make a resignation, tis his right, My calls but vsurpation. Lord Martianus speake. Yet he are me, stay. Patienc sweete wife, Thinkst thou I praise my Crowne aboue thy life, No take it Lords, it hath my trouble bin, And for this Crowne, oh giue me backe my Queene. I know not how I should deserue to dye. My doomes seuerer then my small offence. Aire be made purple with our reaking gore. A third time Lords, I do returne your loue, And wish it with my soule, so heauen were pleasd, My ambitious Brothers had not died for this, But we haue giuen them honorable graues. And mournd their most vntimely funerall, My loued Queen, come seat thee by my side, Partner in all my sorrowes and my ioyes, And you her reconciled Sister sit, By her in second place of maiesty, It ioyes me that you haue outworne your pride. My Lord of Cornwell, whose that whispers to you? Or whats the newes? Weele sit in person on their controuersies, Admit them Cornwell. Tis good you can acquit you, such abuses, Growe in the countrey, and vnknowne to vs: nay then no maruell that so manie poore, starue in the streets and beg from doore, to doore. Then sirha purge you from this countrey blame, Or we will make thee the worlds publike shame. What haue you there in nobodyes pockets. Thou arte Iust we know, All great mens pockets should be lined so.
speeches.Perid: Yonders old Cornwell, come Vïgenius, Weele haue some sport with him: Neuer heereafter beare a souldiers shield, A souldiers sword, nor any other grace, But what is like thine owne, a doubble face.
Brother content. Morrow old gray-beard. And why so. Bridle your spirit. Nay, now youle fall into your techy humor. Is fourth comming. Nay, but farther heare. Ey mary, more of that. A Scepter. And if I make refusall, heauen refuse me. A King. And sit in state. And be obeyed. Seruants homaging, and crying Aue. Not for the world, I long to sit in state, To purse the bountie of our gracious fate. And haue our names ranckt in the course of kings. For his licensious rule, and such abuses As wele pretend gainst him in parliament. Thus wele deuide the Land, all beyond Trent And Humber, shall suffise one moitie: The southpart of the Land shall make the tother, Where we will keepe two Courts, and raigne deuided, Yet as deere louing brothers. Deere sister Q. how are we bound to you, In neerer bonds then a fraternall league, For this your royall practise to raise vs, Vnto the height of honor and estate, Let me no longer breath a prince on earth, Or thinke me woorthy of your regall blood, If we imbrace not this high motion. How shall we quit your loue, when we ascend The state of Elydure. Shees doomd alreadie, and at your dispos • , And we prepard for speedy execution, Of any plot that may availe our pompe, Or throne vs in the state of Brittany. Do but call me king, the charming Spheres so sweetly cannot sing. Oh but wheres our Crowne, that make knees humble, when their soueraignes frowne. And thou that raisest vs, as our best friend, Shall as we mount the like degrees ascend. Well determined, And like a king in Esse, now this night, Lets make a hostile vprore in the Court, Surprize the king, make ceazure of the Crowne, Lay hands vpon the Counsell, least they scape to leuy forces, those Lords that serue the king, and with austere reproofes, punish the hatefull vices of the Land, Must not awe vs, they shall not raigne, we wil, those that applaud vs, raise, despise vs, kill, The king and Crowne is ours. Proclaime me captiue, or a king new crownd, Martianus we. Vn • o whom thou owest thy knee. Our raign beginning hath when his lines end. And more we seeke thy Crowne. We plead our powers & strength, we two must raign. Wilt thou submit thy Crowne? He hates his owne life that aduiseth so. And I another. They shall by heauen. Strike valiant brother king. Now let the king discend to be disposd of At our high pleasure, come giue me the Crowne. Shall I pronounce his sentence. Thy life we graunt thee and that Womans to, But liue deuided you within the tower, You prisoner to that princesse. Cornwell and Martianus you both see, We are possest of this imperiall seate, And you that were sworne liedgemen to the Crowne, Should now submit to vs that owe the same, We know without your graue directions, We cannot with experience guide the land, Therefore weele study to deserue your loues. Receiue our grace, keepe still your offyces, Imbrace these peeres that raisd vs to the throne, Brittaine reioice, and Crowne this happy yeare, Two sonnes at once thine in thy royall sphere. You haue aduisd vs well, it shall be so. Weele haue the Queene set free. In Armes well met, ambitious Peridure, Art thou not proud. Faire is the end Of such as die in honourable warre, Oh far more faire, then on a bed of downe. Such as are apt for tumult. Blushes not Peridure to braue vs so. Peace foole thou doest forget, Tis not an hower since, to our princely eare, Thou saidst thou did desire vs to forbeare. What still. That whosoeuer conquerd, he might gaine. But henceforth we cashiere thee from the filde. then where the fielde consists of such a spirit, He that subdues conquers the Crowne by merit. tis I. Grasse turne to Crimson if vigenius spare it.
Good morrow to you brother Elydure. We shall ha you come out now with some reason that was borne in my great grand sires time. And why father vvinter. You are to saucy Cornwell. Come brother, I am tyrde with reuelling, My last Caranta made me almost breathlesse, Doth not the Kings last wench foote it with art? Nor the rule of Archigallo, Because tis subiect to his libertie. Are they not plotting now for some installement And change of state: old gallants if you be Twill cost your heads. Ey, are you there, that word sounds treason. And a Crowne. These Counsellors are wise, and see in vs More vertue then we in our selues discerne. Would it were come to such election. And were a crowne, a crowne imperiall. Commaund. Our Nobles kneeling. Oh brother, shall we through nice folly Despise the profferd bountie of these Lords? To entertaine forreine Embassadors. Shadow vs State with thy maiesticke wings. Then Archigall, thou that hast sat in pompe And seene me vassaile, shalt behold me crownd, Whilst thou with humble knees vail • t to my state. I know not when. Heare vs excuse our selues. And I. Imbrace it brother, we are all on speed, My princely thought inflam'd with Ardency Of this imperiall state, and Scepterd rule, My kinglie browes, itch for a stately Crowne, This hand to beare a round Monarchall Globe, This the bright sword of Iustice, and stern aw, Deere sister you haue made me all on fire, My kingly thoughts, beyond their bounds aspire. The Queene is yours, the king shalbe depos'd, And she disgraded from all Soueraignty. Heere comes the Lords of this pretended league, How goes our hope, speake valiant English Peeres, Are we in way of Soueraignty, or still stand we Subiects vnto the aw of Elidure. Say Morgan so, and Britains rule is mine. And sit in sta • e. Then they that lifts vs to the imperiall seate, Our powers and will shall study to make great. Now royall sister. Before the king haue notice of our plot, Before the Lords that loue his gouernment, Prepare their opposition. I see a kind of state appeare already In thy maiestick brow, cal in the souldiors, Man the Court gates, barricade al the streets, Defend the waies, the lands and passages, And gi • t the pallace with a treble wall Of armed souldiors, and in dead of night, When all the peeresly drownd in golden sleepe, Sound out a sodaine and a shrill Alarum, to maze them in the midst of horrid dreames. It shal go hard, but I the shrew will tame, trumpets and drums, your dreadfull clamors sound. thou art mine what ere thou be. I Cornwell and thy king. King we seeke thee. We were borne to rule, and homage we disdaine. How saucy Lord? I say that word shall cost old Cornwels life. I am one. So shall all, that doe not prostrate to our homage fall. Shall they not brother king? Rage giue my fury way. Be briefe for Gods sake then, Brother doe. Conuay both hence. Twas not ambition, or the loue of state, that drew vs to this businesse, but the feare, Of Elidurus weakenesse whom in zeale, To the whole land we haue deposd this day, speake, shall we haue your loues? We now are Kings indeede and Brittaine sway, When Cornwell and his brother Viue say Well counseld Cornwell, she shall liue in bondage. Weele haue her guarded, With stricter keeping and seuerer charge. Keepe her in thraldome still, and captiue bands. Before ile stand, Thus for a Cipher with my halfe command, Ile venture all my fortunes, how now pride, Percht on my vpperhand. Vigenius thou salutes me with a title, Most proper to thy selfe, Onely to meet thee on this bed of death, Wherein the Title to the English Crowne, Shall perish with thy selfe. The liues of such as hinder our renowne. Such as you, That to our lawfull Soueraigne are vntrue. Blushes Vigenius at thy ouerthrow, Who wast that told me he would submit. True that I sought to stay. Still playing of the Sicophant. A glose I see to insinuate our good will. the fauour of vs both, that was his trayne. If there be any other of his hart, We giue them free licence to depart. Your words are dangerous, good honest subiect Old reuerent states-man, faithful seruitor, Doe not traduce the King, hees vertuous Or say he tread somewhat besides the line Of vertuous gouernment, his regality Brookes not taxation, kings greatest royalties Are that their subiects must aplaud their deedes, As well as beare them their prerogatiues. Are murall interponents twixt the world, And their proceedings.
My Lords, Princes I should haue said, and after Lords, I am the Vsher and Harbinger vnto the kings most Excellent person and his Maiesty. Or comming fourth, hard by or at hand, will you Put your gestures of attendaunce on, to giue his Maiestie the Bon-ioure. I humblie thanke your highnesse. She is my liege, and mettell I dare warrant. Away you slaues. Heare my aduise my liedge: I know a fellow Thats opposite to Nobody in all thinges: As he affects the poore, this other hates them, Loues vsurie and extortion. Send him straight Into the Country, and vpon my life, Ere many monthes he will deuise some meanes To make that Nobody bankrout, make him flie His Country, and be neuer heard of more. His name is Sombody my liedge. Good day to you both faire Ladies, But fairest of them both my gratious Queene, Good day to your high Maiestie, and madam The royall Lady of great Elidure, My Soueraignes brother, vnto you I wish This morning prooue as gracious and as good. Madam, her highnes gloue. Be patient, I will schoole her. Your excellence greatly forgets your selfe To be so dutilesse vnto the Queene, I haue seene the world, I know what tis to obey, And to commaund. What if it please the Queene That you her subiect should attend on her, And take her gloue vp, is it meete that I Should stoope for yours? You're proud, fie, fie, you're proud. This must not be twixt such two royall sisters As you by marriage are; goe to submit, Her Maiestie is easie to forgiue. Beare witnes Madam, Ile goe tell the King That they speake treason. I hope not so. Nay then Ile take your parts, and ioyne with you ▪ I hope my Lady Is not of their minds. My most gratious Queene, What I did speake in reprehensiue sort, Was more because her Maiestie was present Then any offence of yours, and so esteeme it, God knowes I loue your highnes, and these Lords. Nay, then as I did lately to her Highnes, I must admonish you, diected Lady You doe forget your selfe, and where you are, Duty is debt, and it is fit since now You are a subiect, to beare humble thoughts: Follow my counsell Lady and submit, Her Maiestie no doubt will pardon it. Which way so ere I goe, I haue it heere, whether it ebbe or flowe. Madam, it is her Highnes will be pleas'd. Shall it be so my Liedge. You are not wise, deiected as you are To bandie braues against her Maiestie, You must consider you are now her subiect, Your tongue is bounded by the awe of dutie, Fie, fie, I needes must chide you, since I see You are so sawcie with her soueraigntie. Fie madam fie, fore God you are too blame In presence of my soueraigne ladie Queene To be thus rude, it would become you better To shew more dutie to her Maiestie. Yes, when your husband was my King you were. But now the streame is turnd, and the States currant, Runnes all to Archigallo, blame not mee, Wisedome nere lou'd declined Maiestie. Madam, you are not wise to grieue at that Heauen hath decreed, and the state yeelded to, No doubt her Maiestie will vse you well. Your lookes declard the passion of your hart, They were all fire. Wilt please your high imperiall Maiestie Commaund my seruice, I am humbly yours. My Lords receiue the crowne of Elydure, Faire hopefull blossoms of our future peace, Happy am I, that I but liue to see, the Land ruld by your dubble Soueraignty. Nay Madam, now I needes must tell your grace, You wrong these kings, forget both time and place, It is not as it was, now you must bowe, Vnto this dubble state ile shew you how. I haue prouided, you will let me share, Of the Grand-benefit you get by dice, Deceitfull Cards, and other cozening games you bring into the Court. Twas I my Lord. True my good Lord. Where is the Lady Elidor I pray. Mercy my Soueraigne.
Good morrow to our soueraigne Archigallo.
Morrow. Lets see those papers. A controuersie betwixt the Lord Morgan and the Lord Malgo, concerning their Ty tles to the Southerne Island. We know this cause and what their titles be. You claime it by inheritance. You by the marriage of Lord Morgans mother, To whom it was left ioynture. Whose euidence is strongest, to which part Inclines the censures of our learned Iudges. What I determine then youle yeeld vnto. Then that Southerne Ile we take to our protection, and make you Lord gouernor thereof. Replie not, I but take it to my selfe Because I would not haue dissention betwixt two peeres, I loue to see you friends, And now the Islands mine, your quarrell ends. Whats next. A poore Nothern mans humble petition. Which is the plaintiue? Is this true my Wench. Thou art a proper fellow, and this wench is thine by lawfull marriage. Is not this Lasse a pretty Neat browne Wrench? Fellow, how long hast thou been married? Didst neuer lie with thy wife? Harke my wench, wilt leaue these rusticke fellowes & stay with me? Why Ile make thee a Lady. Thou shalt. What we will, we will, away with those slaues. Whats that to thee, old doting Lord forbeare. Whats heere? complaints against one Nobody, For ouermuch releeuing of the poore, Helping distressed prisoners, entertayning Extrauagants and vagabonds, what fellowes this? Ile haue none such as he within my kingdome, Hee shall be banisht. VVhat doost thou call his name. Seeke out that Sombody, wele send him straight, VVhat other matters stay to be decided Determine you, and you, the rest may follow To giue attendance. Oh monstrous brothers. As vild traitors. And when must this be doone, when shall my crowne Be parted and deuided into halfes. You raigne on this side Humber, you beyond The riuer Trent, when doe you take your states, Sit crownd and scepterd to receiue our homage, Our dutie, and our humble vassalage. Nor you? But I know when you shall repent your pride. Nor will we vse delayes in our reuenge, Ambitious boyes, we doome you prisonment, Your Pallace royall shall a Iaile be made, Your thrones a dungeon, and your scepters Irons, In which wele bound your proude aspiring thoughts: A way with them, we will not mount our chayre Ti • l their best hopes be changd to blacke despaire. That shall our further leysures arbitrate, Our eares are deafe to all excusiue pleas, Come vnambitious brother Elidurus, Helpe vs to lauish our abundant treasures, In masks, sports, reuells, riots, and strange pleasures. Then giue it me; vse not the common sleights, To pittie one, and keepe away his right. Seest thou these ragges, doe they become my person? O Elidure, take pittie on my state, Let me not still liue thus infortunate. What shall I die then? welcome be that fate Rather then still liue in this wretched state. I am thy King. Let it be so, Death is the happy period of all woe. The wretch thats torne vpon the torturing wrack, Feeles not more de •••• sh torment then my hart. When I but call to minde my tirannie, I record heauen my Lords, my brothers fight, The pittie that he takes of my distresse, Your loue and true allegiance vnto him, Hath wrought in me a reconciled spirit, I doe confesse my sinne, and freely say, I did deserue to be deposd. By heauen I not desire it. And happie Archigallo that haue rangd From sin, to sin, and now at last am changd. My Lords and friends, the wrongs that you haue seene In me, my future vertues shall redeeme. Come gentle brother, pittie that should rest In women most, is harbor'd in thy brest. To heauen, and my kind brother Elidure, Faire Queene we owe chiefe thanks for this our greatnes, Next them, these honourable Lords. Set on there.
My liege I do. To a Sicophant, a courtly parasite. That will I. Then weele embrace his gouernment. Health to the Queene, and happines to her That must change states with you, and once more raigne Queene of this Land. Euen in the woods where we did hunt the stagge, There did the tender harted Elidure Meete his distressed Brother, and so wrought By his importunate speech with all his Peeres, That after much deniall, yet at last They yeelded their allegiance to your Lord, Whom now we must acknowledge our dread King, And you our princelie Queene. Yet for his Princelie worth that made you Queene Respect her as the wife of Elidure. And so is Morgan, for he scornes delayes. A strang fight, my Lord is breathlesse. Cards of aduantage with such cheating tricks, Brought euen amongst the noblest of the land, And when these cosening shifts are once discouered, There is no cheater found saue No-body.
True gratious Soueraigne. Passe vpon our swords, You old exchecker of all flatterie, I tell thee Archigallo shall be deposd, And thou disroab'd of all thy dignitie. Thus it shall be, vse my direction. In Court and country I am Sombody, And therefore apt and fit to be employed: Goe thou in secrete beeing a subtile knaue. But if my breeches had as much cloth in them, as euer was drawne betwixt Kendall and Canning street, they were scarce great enough to hold all the wrongs that I must pocke • : Fie, fie, how I am slaunderd through the world. Nobody keepes tall fellowes at his heeles, Yet if you meete a crew of rogues and beggars, Aske who they serue, theile aunswere Nobody. Your Caualiers and swaggerers bout the towne, That dominere in Tauerns, sweare and stare, Vrge them vpon some termes, theile turne their malice To me, and say theile fight with Nobody, Or if they fight, and Nobody by chaunce Come in to part them, I am sure to pay for it, And Nobody be hurt when they scape scotfree: And not the dastardst coward in the world But dares about with me. What shall I doe? Why so sir? And thou sayest true in that my honest seruaunt, Besides, I am in great especiall grace With the King Archigallo that now raignes In tiranny, and strange misgouerment, Nobody loues him, and he loues Nobody. And though a man haue doone a thousand mischiefes, And come to proue the forfeit made to law, If he can proue he hath wrong'd Nobody, No man can touch his life. Oh Maister you are halfe hangd. Besides, you haue one commoditie Maister, which none hath besides you, if you should loue the most fickle & in constants wench that is in the world, sheele be true to No body, therefore constant to you. O Maister, there I am sure Nobody may haue anie thing without mony, Nobody may come out of the Tauerne without pay ing his reckoning at his pleasure. Of Nobodies making, that will be rare. Why Nobody receaues them. You knaue: or as the world goes, Somebody receiues all, and Nobody is blamd for it. Doe not you knowe that? theres not an orphants por tion lost out of the Chamber, but Nobody has got it, no Corne transported without warrant, but Nobody has donne it, no goods stolne but by Nobody, no extortion without Nobody: and but that truth will come to light, fewe wenches got with child, but with Nobody. I thinke Somebody had a hand in't, but Nobody some times paies for the nursing of it. Tis a mad world Maister. Heere they be Sir. Tis great pitty my Maister has Nobody, and so kind a hart. Yes Maister, I Nobodies man. My harts lower then my hofe, for mine it at my heel, but whersoeuer it is, it is a true hart, and so is not somb.

What on Nobody, giue me my sword, my morglay, My friends, you that doe know how innocent I am, Draw in my quarrell, succor Nobody, What Nobody, but Nobody remaining. Stand to me nobly then, and feare them not, Thy Maister Nobody, can take no wounds, Nobody is no coward, Nobody Dares fight withall the world. What are they gonne, then Citty now adew, Since I haue taken such great iniury, For my good life within thy gouernment: No more will Nobody be charitable, No mote will Nobody relieue the poore, Honor your Lord, and Maister Somebody, For Somebody is he that wrongs you all. Ile to the Court the changing of the ayre, May peraduenture change my iniuries, And if I speede no better being there, Yet say that Nobody liu'd euery where. I thanke you sir.

Why Nobody. I thanke you sir, and were your beere tems water, Yet No-body would pledge you, to you sir. I sir, too long, vnlesse my entertaine Had bin more pleasing, for my life is sought, I am a harmelesse well dispos'd plaine man, That iniure none, yet what so ere is done Amisse in London, is impos'd on me, Be it lying, secret theft, or any thing They call abuse, tis done by No-body, I am pursued by all, and now am come, To see what safety is within the Court For a plaine fellow. O do not blame me sir, Being pursued I fled, comming though Poules, There No-body kneeld downe to say his prayers, And was deuout I wis, comming through Fleetstreet, There at a tauern doore two swaggerers Were fighting, being attacht, twas askt who gaue The first occasion, twas answered nobody, The guilt was laid on me, which made me fly To the Thems side, desired a Waterman, To row me thence away to Charing-crosse, He askt me for his fare, I answered him I had no money, whats your name quoth he, I told him No-body, then he bad me welcome, Said he would carry No-body for nothing. From thence I went To see the law Courts held at Westminster, There meeting vvith a friend, I straight vvas askt If I had any sute, I ansvvered, yes, Marry I vvanted money, sir quoth he, For you, because your name is No-body I vvill sollicit law, and no-body Assure your selfe, shall thriue by sutes in Lavv, I thankt him, and so came to see the court, Where I am very much beholding to your kindnesse. I thinke youle sooner kill me then any body, But let me rise againe. Why then let me sir, I am No-body, Thanks honest seruant. For this ile carry thee into the Court, Where thou shalt see thy Maister No-body Hath friends will bid him welcome, so farewell, O excellent, admirable, and beyond comparison, I thinke my shape inchants them. Not I, I am an innocent, no Cheater, no Cozener, but a simple honest man, hunted from place to place by some-body.

speeches.1 Man: Faith sir I haue cause, I haue lent a friend of mine a hun dred pounde, and haue Nobodyes worde for the payment, bill, nor bond, nor any thing to shew. Ey, say you so, nay then lets drinke downe sorrow, If none would lend, then Nobody should borrow.
speeches.Nobody: Yet there's one keepes a good tongue in his head, That can giue Nobody a good report, I am beholding to him for his praise: But since my man so much commends the Cittie, Ile thether, and to purchase me a name, Take a large house of infinite receipt, There keepe a table for all good spirits, And all the chimneyes shall cast smoake at once: There Ile giue schollers pensions, Poets gold, Arts their deserts, Philosophy due praise, Learning his merrit, and all worth his meede. There Ile release poore prisoners from their dungeons. Pay Creditors the debts of other men, And get my selfe a name mongst Cittizens, That after times pertakers of all blisse, May thus record, Nobody did all this. Country farewell, whose slaunderous tongues I slie, The Cittie now shall lift my name on hie.
speeches.Sombody: Whether Ile follow thee with Swallowes wings, And nimble expedition, there to raise New brawles and rumors to eclipse thy praise. Those subtile, slie insinuating fellowes Whom Sombody hath sent into the country, To rack, transport, extort, and to oppresse, VVill I call home, and all their wits employ Against this publique Benefactor, knowne Honest, for all the rumors by vs sowne. But howsoeuer, I am sworne his foe, And opposite to all his meriting deedes, This way must doe, though my deuining thoughts This augurie amidsts their changes haue, That Sombody will at length be proou'd a knaue.
speeches.Queene: Those greetings from the Lady Elidure VVould pleasingly sound in our princely eares. Speake that againe, ô I will blesse my fate, If once more I supply my former state. Now minion, Ile cry quittance with your pride, And make you stoope at our imperiall side ▪ But tell me Morgan by what accident You met with my beloued Archigallo? Restraine her good my Lord. Our shoe string is vntied, stoope minion, stoope. Bring me the worke there, I will taske you to, That by the howre spin it, I charge you doe. What newes with Cornwell, why so sad my Lord? O my hart. Now as you loue me let no helping hand Preserue life in me, I had rather die Then loose the title of my soueraigntie.
speeches.Lady: Such greetings from great Archigalloes queene VVould be most gratious to our princely eare. Is my Coach ready, where are all my men That should attend vpon our awfull frowne, VVhat not one neere? Painted Maiestie be gone, I am not to be countercheckt by any. VVhich of you will perswade my Elidure To take vpon him Englands royaltie. This mildnes in him makes me so despisd By the proude Queene, and by her fauourits. My Lord and husband, with your leaue this booke Is fitter for an Vniuersitie Then to be lookt on, and the Crowne so neere: You know these Lords for tyrannie haue sworne To banish Archigallo from the throne, And to invest you in the royaltie: VVill you not thanke them, and with bounteous hands Sprinckle their greatnes with the names of Earles, Dukes, Marquesses, and other higher termes. Come haue you done your taske, now doe you see What tis to be so proude of Maiestie, We must take vp your gloue, and not be thought Worthy the name of Sister, thus you minx Ile teach you ply your worke, and thanke me to, This paines will be your owne another day. My Lord, if she continue these proude termes, I giue you libertie to punish her. Ile not maintaine my prisoner and my slaue To raile gainst any one that honours me. O I could teare my haire, base Elidure To wrong himselfe, and make a slaue of me. Thou Screchowle, Rauen, vglie throated slaue ▪ Theres for thy newes. VVell saiest thou: no I looke that she should treble All the disgraces I haue layd on her. I shall turne Laundresse now, and learne to starch, And set and poke, and pocket vp such basenes As neuer princesse did: did you obserue What lookes I cast at Elidure my husband? Ile rather stoope to death thou moone-like Queene, New changd, and yet so proude: theres those are made For flexure, let them stoope, thus much Ile doe, You are my Queene, tis but a debt I owe. A distaffe and a spindle, so indeed I told you this, Diana be my speede. Now if it be thy will, sweet blessed heauen Take him to mercie. Take backe your Distaffe yet, wele stay our rage, We will forbeare our spleene for charitie And loue vnto the dead, till you haue hearsd Your husbands bones, conduct her Lords away, Our pride though eager, yet for foode shall stay. We doe commaund what we well know youle doe, Follow the stronger part, and cleaue thereto. What traitrous hand dares interdict our way? Wilt thou be made a stale, Shall this proud Woman, and these boyes preuaile? Shal I for them be made a publike scorne, Oh hadst thou buried bin, assoone as borne, How happy had I bin. Oh monstrous lie.
